problem: Existing VLM-based ObjectNav methods use the VLM passively (scene description, frontier scoring) with rigid prompts and no memory. This leads to inefficient exploration, oscillation and loops in visually repetitive places such as corridors.
motivation: Zero-shot ObjectNav needs both semantic common sense and spatial awareness, and VLMs carry rich contextual knowledge that is underused. The authors observe that agents without temporal context oscillate between frontiers, and that a VLM that reasons step by step about room type and target likelihood makes more coherent decisions.
key_idea: Make a VLM (LLaVA-1.6 7B) the high-level strategist of a VLFM-style frontier exploration pipeline, using structured chain-of-thought prompts, a 10-step action history, and a top-down obstacle map alongside the egocentric view.
insight: Removing the action history causes by far the largest drop (HM3D SR 54.3 to 44.0, Gibson SR 80.2 to 65.0), so loop avoidance and temporal context matter most. CoT depth gives a monotonic gain (No CoT to Full CoT: HM3D SR 51.2 to 54.3, SPL 29.0 to 31.1), while the obstacle map adds only a small gain (HM3D SR 53.6 to 54.3). Caveat: the ablations use a 50-episode subset, so small differences are noisy.
method: Frontier waypoint generation: builds an obstacle map from depth, detects frontier midpoints as waypoint candidates, and uses the VER policy for low-level motion.

VLM value map: LLaVA-1.6 outputs action scores (forward/backward/left/right) that are projected onto the map and weighted by a viewing-confidence term c=exp(-λd)·cos²(θ/(θfov/2)·π/2). Overlapping observations are fused by confidence-weighted averaging of value and confidence, and frontiers are ranked by value.

Structured CoT prompt: the VLM is led through four steps: identify the room type, judge whether the target can be there, check whether the target is visible, then recommend an action and give scores. It is instructed to keep its reasoning consistent.
Action history: the last 10 actions are inserted into the prompt with instructions to avoid repetitive actions; a backup plan repeats the last successful action if the agent still gets stuck.
Top-down map parsing: the VLM receives a top-down obstacle map (obstacles in gray, heading arrow) as a second image, explained only via the prompt without any map training.
Goal navigation hybrid: the target is detected with YOLOv7 or Grounding-DINO, verified by the VLM, and segmented with Mobile-SAM for the final approach.

setting.backbone: LLaVA-1.6 7B (frozen, prompted) + YOLOv7/Grounding-DINO/Mobile-SAM detectors + VER low-level policy
setting.observation: egocentric RGB + depth (for obstacle map) + pose, plus a top-down obstacle map image
setting.action_space: low-level forward/turn/stop, guided by 2D frontier waypoints; the VLM's forward/backward/left/right scores feed the value map

numbers_note: Splits are described only as the standard Habitat challenge validation splits, hence 'val'. The ablation tables (50-episode subset) repeat the full-framework numbers identical to the main table, so they are not listed separately.
results: Zero-shot with a 7B VLM, the method reaches HM3D SR 54.3 / SPL 31.1 and MP3D SR 36.0 / SPL 17.7, giving the best SPL on both. On HM3D it also beats VLFM (52.5/30.4) and GAMap (53.1/26.0); on Gibson it is 80.2/53.0, below VLFM (84.0/52.2 SR) and GAMap (85.7/55.5). MP3D SR is slightly below VLFM's 36.4.
limitations: High computational cost of VLMs limits real-time use, and the prompt is hand-engineered rather than optimized.
Ablations use only a 50-episode subset with no error bars, and gains over VLFM are small (about 1-2 points), so significance is unclear.
Failure analysis shows the agent still suffers from loops, missed in-view targets, cross-floor navigation and annotation issues; no real-robot tests or code are given.
